newsitem.title: USA: Clinton-Dole to debate one-on-one without Perot.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Dole to debate one-on-one without Perot.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's representatives on Saturday scrapped their hopes of including Ross Perot in presidential debates, agreeing to a one-on-one format with Republican nominee Bob Dole who had refused to share the stage with the feisty Texas billionaire.

After more than nine hours of talks, negotiators for Clinton and Dole agreed to hold two 90-minute debates. The agreement also calls for one debate between Vice President Al Gore and Dole's running mate Jack Kemp.
The first presidential debate will be held on Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, followed by the vice presidential match up in St. Petersburg, Florida on Oct. 9.
The last presidential debate will be held in San Diego on October 16, and, unlike the previous debates, will have a town hall format that allows participants to directly question the nominees.

The Clinton campaign tried to keep Reform Party candidate Perot and his running mate Pat Choate in the mix, but the Dole campaign was flatly oppossed to their inclusion, said Clinton's lead negotiator, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor.

"We're sorry Mr. Perot and Mr. Choate are not in the debates, we did everything we can, but the president said there has to be debates, we cannot allow these to go by the board. They are in the best interest of the people," Kantor said.
Analysts had said the Clinton campaign favoured Perot's presence in the debates because he would tend to draw votes away from Dole, which is why Dole opposed Perot's presence.

"I think what we have come up with is acceptable to the Dole campaign," said Dole's chief negotiator, former South Carolina Gov. Carroll Campbell. "The fact is we have one-on-one debates with the president of the United States and Senator Dole and that is what we wanted and we wanted a minimum of two of them."
Cambell said the Dole camp became willing to accept the town hall format for one debate when it became clear Perot was out of the mix.

"We had a very substantive discussion off and on all day," Campbell, who also heads the American Council of Life Insurance, told reporters. "We did not agree on everything. We worked it out as we went along."
The gregarious Clinton is widely thought to have the edge in the more spontaneous town hall-type debates, and his side argued vigorously for a format that served him well in 1992.

The three cities chosen have never before hosted presidential debates. Kantor said he was "delighted to be in California anytime we can go there. We've spent some time there as some of you have noticed."
Clinton holds a whopping lead in polls over Dole in the state, the biggest prize in the November election, and he has visited there dozens of times during his presidency.
Negotiators said they expect to agree on moderators before Tuesday when both sides were to sign the debate agreement.

The Clinton team originally wanted two debates lasting two hours each with one including Perot, and one vice presidential debate. Dole, trailing in the polls, had wanted three 75-minute presidential debates and one vice presidential debate, with Perot excluded.

On Friday, Perot lodged a formal complaint with the Federal Election Commission. His campaign said it would file a lawsuit on Monday over the Commission on Presidential Debates' decision to bar him from the debates.

The debate commission, which makes non-binding recommendations, last Tuesday said Perot and Choate should be excluded from debates, declaring the Perot ticket had no real chance of winning the Nov. 5 election.
